modules.title: World-championship decisive moments
modules.summary: The critical position of title games from 1969 to 2024, solved as challenges: find the move that decided the match game, and check what the engine says about it.
modules.source: Aagaard, Grandmaster Preparation: Thinking Inside the Box (critical decisions); games Spassky-Petrosian 1969 game 19, Fischer-Spassky 1972 game 10, Carlsen-Karjakin 2016 rapid game 4, Ding-Nepomniachtchi 2023 game 12, Nepomniachtchi-Ding 2023 rapid game 4, Gukesh-Ding 2024 game 11, Ding-Gukesh 2024 game 14; engine checks with Stockfish 16 at depth 16 to 24

lessons.title: Fischer 1972: the critical decision
lessons.objective: Recognise a critical position, where the best move is far ahead of the second, and spend your time there.

sections.md:
Aagaard sorts decisions into four types: automatic, simple, critical and strategic. A critical decision is one where the gap between the best move and the second-best move is large. A game often turns on a handful of them. Spend your clock there.

Signs of a critical position:

1. A piece of yours is attacked twice or pinned, and the problem will not wait.
2. A forcing sequence exists, and it changes the material or the structure for good.
3. The quiet moves all fail to the same opponent's resource.

Fischer-Spassky, game 10 of the 1972 match, move 30. The white knight on e5 is attacked by the queen and the rook, and ...f6 is coming. Fischer cashed in with 30.Bxf7+ and reached an ending with two rooks against rook and bishop. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 gives about +0.5 after 30.Bxf7+ and about -3.5 after the best quiet move, 30.Bd5. That four-pawn gap is the definition of critical.

lessons.title: Spassky-Petrosian 1969: open the lines, then strike
lessons.objective: In an opposite-castling race, give pawns to open files towards the king, then calculate the knight blow that finishes it.

sections.md:
Game 19 of the 1969 match. The kings stand on opposite wings. In such races, pawns are worth less than open files: each pawn that opens a line towards the enemy king brings a piece into the attack.

Spassky gave the g-pawn (15.g4 Nxg4) to open the g-file for his rook, pushed 18.f5 to open the f-file, and gave the e-pawn (21.e5 dxe5) to free e4 for his knight. Stockfish 16 at depth 16 rates 15.g4 and 18.f5 as the best moves.

Then two knight moves end the game: 22.Ne4, heading for f6 and g5, and 24.Ng5. Stockfish 16 rates both as clearly best.

Count the open lines towards each king before you count the pawns.

lessons.title: Ding 2023: the counter-blow and the refusal to repeat
lessons.objective: Find the central counter-blow when the opponent's attack is one tempo slow, and judge when to avoid a repetition.

sections.md:
Two decisions from the 2023 match.

Game 12. Both kings were weakened. Black's queen and rook aimed at the white king along the h-file. Then 34...f5 left the e6-pawn without the f-pawn's protection. Ding struck in the centre with 35.Rxe6: the rook takes the pawn, the d-pawn advances with check, and the black attack is too slow. Stockfish 16 at depth 22: about +5.3 after 35.Rxe6, about -2.3 after 35.gxf5.

Rapid tiebreak, game 4. Ding, with Black, could head for a repetition with 46...Kg8. He played 46...Rg6 and won. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates both moves 0.00. The choice was practical, not forced: Black had an extra pawn, passed a- and c-pawns and a safe king, so he could play on without risk.

Two lessons: calculate the counter-blow as a race, and do not take a repetition when you can press at no cost.

lessons.title: Clinchers: 50.Qh6+ and 29.Qxc6
lessons.objective: See the final blow that comes from piece placement: open files for the rooks, and an x-ray through the opponent's queen.

sections.md:
Two title games, each finished by a queen move.

Carlsen-Karjakin, rapid tiebreak game 4, 2016. White's rooks are on c8 and f5, the black king on h7. 50.Qh6+ gives the queen: after 50...Kxh6 the rook mates on h8, after 50...gxh6 the other rook mates on f7. The blow works because both rooks already stand on open lines.

Gukesh-Ding, game 11, 2024. White's long queenside plan (b4-b5-b6, Rb5, Nc5) pinned Black down on b7 and c6. Ding's 28...Qc8 left the queen guarding both the knight on c6 (with the b7-pawn) and the rook on b8, while the bishop on g2 looks at c6 through the white queen. 29.Qxc6 wins material in every line.

In both games the final move is short. The work was the piece placement before it. Before you look for the blow, look at your pieces' lines.

lessons.title: Ding-Gukesh 2024: the title decided in a pawn ending
lessons.objective: Know when a rook trade turns a drawn rook-and-bishop ending into a lost pawn ending, from both sides of the board.

sections.md:
Game 14, the last classical game of the 2024 match, score level. Rook and bishop each; Black has one extra kingside pawn. Stockfish 16 rates the position as a draw with normal moves.

Then 55.Rf2 offered the rook trade. After 55...Rxf2 56.Kxf2 Bd5! Black forces the bishops off as well, and the pawn ending is lost for White: Black's king takes the opposition and the extra pawn decides.

The rule behind it: before you trade into a pawn ending, count it to the end. A pawn ending forgives nothing; a rook or bishop ending often forgives a lot. With one pawn less, the defender should keep pieces on the board.

Stockfish 16 at depth 20: 55.Rf2 is about -7; quiet moves such as 55.Bg2 or 55.Kf1 hold at about -0.2.

lessons.title: Tal: sacrifice, then make the defender prove it
lessons.objective: Judge a sacrifice by the problems it sets and by the engine's verdict, and see why the defender's task is harder than the attacker's.

sections.md:
Some of Tal's sacrifices do not survive an engine check, and he won with them anyway. Two reasons. The defender must find several only-moves in a row, with the clock running. And the attacker's alternatives were often no better.

Botvinnik-Tal, game 6 of the 1960 match, move 21. Black is under pressure. Tal played 21...Nf4: a knight for pawns, the long diagonal for the g7-bishop and an exposed white king. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates Black slightly worse after it (about -0.9), but every other move is worse still (about -1.05). The sacrifice was the best move in a worse position.

Tal-Larsen, Candidates 1965, move 16. Tal gave a knight on d5 to open the e-file. Stockfish 16 at depth 20 gives about -0.6 after 16.Nd5 and +0.6 after the quiet 16.Ne2. Objectively dubious; in practice, Larsen lost.

Use the engine after the game to learn which sacrifices were sound. At the board, ask: how many only-moves must he find?

lessons.title: Kasparov's immortal: quiet moves inside the king hunt
lessons.objective: Keep the initiative after a sacrifice by finding the quiet move that attacks while the king is chased.

sections.md:
Kasparov-Topalov, Wijk aan Zee 1999. 24.Rxd4 gives a rook to drag the black king across the board.

What the engine says. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates 24.Rxd4 as White's best move, about -0.3: the position before it was already difficult for White. The correct defence was 24...Kb6. Topalov took the rook (24...cxd4), and after 25.Re7+ White was about one pawn better.

Then the king walks from a7 to d1. With the black king on d1, White has only a queen, a rook and a bishop left, and Black threatens checks. Two quiet moves decide:

1. 36.Bf1 attacks the queen on c4 and keeps e2 covered.
2. 37.Rd7 deflects the black rook from the d-file, and White wins the h8-rook with the queen.

In a king hunt, look for the move that is not a check: the attacker's pieces often need one tempo to reach their best squares.

lessons.title: Shirov's 47...Bh3: a bishop for a king route
lessons.objective: In an opposite-coloured bishop ending, give the bishop when it opens the road for your king to escort two passed pawns.

sections.md:
Opposite-coloured bishops usually draw. The defender's bishop and king blockade the passed pawns on squares the other bishop cannot attack.

Topalov-Shirov, Linares 1998. Black has passed pawns on a4 and d5. The black king wants to support them via f5 and e4, but its own bishop stands on f5.

47...Bh3 gives the bishop. After 48.gxh3 the black king walks f5, e4, d3, and the two passed pawns, supported by the king, are too much for White's bishop.

What the engine says. In a multi-line search Stockfish 16 rates several bishop moves at about +1 for Black. Searched one move at a time to depth 22, it gives about +5 after 47...Bh3 and about +1.5 after 47...Be4. The sacrifice is the clearest win.

In an ending, count tempi for the king, not material.

modules.title: Engine-era ideas: AlphaZero and Deep Blue
modules.summary: What the machines changed: the exchange sacrifice for a long-term bind, the king as an attacker once the queens are off, the h-pawn as a lever, and the defender's resources a human missed.
modules.source: Sadler and Regan, Game Changer (2019) on AlphaZero's style; AlphaZero-Stockfish 8 games published by DeepMind with the 2018 Science paper; Deep Blue-Kasparov 1997 game 2; Ding-Nepomniachtchi 2023 game 6; engine checks with Stockfish 16

lessons.title: AlphaZero: the exchange for a bind
lessons.objective: Give the exchange when it locks the opponent's king and pieces for good, and judge it by mobility, not material.

sections.md:
AlphaZero's published games against Stockfish 8 show a style built on mobility: material given for activity, with no immediate tactics to win it back.

In this game (a Nimzo-English, from the games DeepMind released in 2018), White's rook on g5 is attacked by the knight on e6. AlphaZero left it there and played 33.Rf6, pinning the g6-pawn against the black king. After 33...Nxg5 34.hxg5+ Kh7 35.f4 the pawns on f4 and g5 and the bishop on the long diagonal lock Black's king and rooks in. Material: a rook for a knight. Mobility: White's pieces have squares, Black's have few.

Stockfish 16 at depth 22 agrees with AlphaZero: 33.Rf6 is the best move, about +1.5, against 0.0 for the next best.

Judge an exchange sacrifice by three questions: which enemy pieces lose their squares, which of my pawns become strong, and can the opponent ever give the exchange back?

lessons.title: AlphaZero: the king walks in
lessons.objective: Use the king as an attacking piece once the queens are off, and squeeze the opponent until he can only shuffle.

sections.md:
Classical advice: in the middlegame, keep the king safe; in the endgame, centralise it. AlphaZero pushed the second half further: with queens off, its king walked into the opponent's half while rooks and bishops were still on the board.

In this Caro-Kann Advance from the 2018 set, AlphaZero traded queens on move 27. Then:

1. 37.Kg3, 38.Kh4, 39.Kg5: the king walks to g5, next to Black's weak pawns on g6 and h5.
2. 43.a6 breaks the black king's cover: after 43...bxa6 the bishop takes a7 with check two moves later.
3. From move 47 to 57 Black only shuffles bishop, king and rooks while White improves.
4. 61.Rxg6 cashes in.

Stockfish 16 at depth 16 rates 39.Kg5 and 43.a6 as the best moves, but only by a small margin: this is a squeeze, not a combination.

lessons.title: The h-pawn as a lever
lessons.objective: Push the rook pawn to fix or open the opponent's kingside when his pieces cannot answer it.

sections.md:
Sadler and Regan's study of AlphaZero, Game Changer, describes one of its habits: pushing the rook pawn up the board, even in front of its own castled king. The pawn fixes enemy pawns, takes squares from enemy pieces, or opens a file.

Ding-Nepomniachtchi, game 6 of the 2023 match, shows the idea in a London System. Black has traded his dark-squared bishop. White plays 21.h4 and later 27.h5: the pawn drives the black bishop from g6 and fixes the h6-pawn in front of the black king. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates 21.h4 as White's best move, but only by about 0.15: a long-term idea, not a combination.

The attack ends with a knight blow. On move 43 the knight jumps to g6, next to the black king, and the threat Qxg7 mate comes before Black's a-pawn can queen.

lessons.title: Deep Blue 1997: restraint, and the draw that was missed
lessons.objective: Prefer the move that keeps the opponent without counterplay, and as a defender, check every check before you resign.

sections.md:
Game 2 of the 1997 match teaches two things.

First, Deep Blue played like a positional player. On move 37 it could go after Black's queenside pawns with 37.Qb6. It played 37.Be4 instead, which blockades e4 and takes away Black's only counterplay, the push ...e4. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates both moves at about +1 (37.Be4 slightly higher). The lesson is restraint: the move that removes counterplay is often worth as much as a pawn.

Second, Kasparov resigned after 45.Ra6, in a position where 45...Qe3! holds the draw. Stockfish 16 at depth 24: about +0.2 for White (a draw) after 45...Qe3, about +4.4 after the next best move.

The defender's routine before resigning: list every check, every capture and every threat against the enemy king. Here the white king on f1 is short of cover, and the black queen can reach e3 with tempo.

lessons.title: Capablanca 1924: the king is worth two pawns
lessons.objective: In a rook ending, give pawns to bring the king forward when king, rook on the seventh and a passed pawn create mating threats.

sections.md:
Capablanca-Tartakower, New York 1924, is one of the most quoted rook endings in chess literature.

White has a rook on the seventh rank and a pawn on g5, but Black threatens ...Rxc3+. Capablanca played 35.Kg3: he let Black take both pawns with check, because his king reaches h4, g5 and f6. There, king, rook and the g-pawn create mating threats against the black king on the back rank.

Stockfish 16 at depth 22: about +2.2 after 35.Kg3, about +0.2 after the next best move.

Three rook-ending rules in one game:

1. A rook on the seventh rank is worth about a pawn (Fine's rule of thumb).
2. An active king is worth more than a pawn, sometimes two.
3. A far-advanced passed pawn, supported by king and rook, outweighs the opponent's material.

lessons.title: Anand-Carlsen 2013: the one drawing move
lessons.objective: Defend a long rook ending against an active king and two pawns, and find the single move that keeps the draw.

sections.md:
Game 6 of the 2013 match. From a quiet Berlin, Carlsen won material and walked his king to e3, into White's camp. On move 60 the pawns are level, three each, but Black's king, rook and the f- and h-pawns attack White's kingside.

On move 60 Anand had one drawing move. 60.b4! starts the queenside pawns at once: Black's attack still costs him tempi, and White's counterplay arrives in time. Anand played 60.Ra4?, one tempo too slow, and lost.

Stockfish 16 at depth 24: about 0.0 after 60.b4, about -4.3 after 60.b3, and worse after every other move, including the game's 60.Ra4 (about -4.9).

The defender's rule in rook endings: counterplay with your own passed pawns is worth more than passive defence. Count the tempi of both pawn races before every move.

sections.md:
Shereshevsky's endgame rule: do not hurry. When the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece first. Then play the break.

Game 10 of the 2016 match. Carlsen needed a win. Queens came off on move 24; Black's weak pawns on e6 and d5 were blockaded, his king was kept away from the kingside, and White's knight took c5.

For thirty moves Carlsen improved: king, rooks, knight, and the pawn moves b4 and a5 to fix the queenside. Only on move 57 did he break with b4-b5. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates 57.b5 as the best move (about +1.9, against about +1.1 for the next best).

The checklist before a break:

1. Is every piece on its best square?
2. Are the opponent's pieces at their most passive?
3. After the break, which file or square do I get, and can he use the open line first?
